title: Three sisters polyculture
subtitle: Maize, beans, and squash in one bed, each supporting the others.
excerpt: Three sisters is a traditional North American polyculture combining maize, climbing beans, and squash in one bed. The maize supports the beans, the beans fix nitrogen, and the squash shades the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture.
sourceNotes: Agricultural practice documented by USDA and university extension services (University of Vermont Extension). Traditional Haudenosaunee / Iroquois companion planting practice widely documented in American agricultural literature. Adaptation for UK climate informed by RHS guidance on sweetcorn and squash timing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Growing two or more plant species together in the same bed so that they support each other. Contrasts with monoculture, where only one species is grown. Benefits can include reduced pest pressure, better use of light, and improved soil fertility.

The process by which certain plants (primarily legumes like beans and clover) convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use, via bacteria living on their roots. Excess nitrogen becomes available in the soil when the plant dies or its roots are cut.

content.text: from North American growing traditions. Three crops go in the same bed: maize, climbing beans, and squash. The maize gives the beans a living pole to climb. The beans are
. The squash covers the ground with broad leaves and keeps weeds down.

In the UK, the main challenge is timing. Sweetcorn (the traditional maize substitute) needs a warm, sunny summer to set cobs reliably. In cooler areas or poor summers, a three sisters bed may produce good beans and squash but disappointing corn. In a warm southern UK summer, the whole system works well.

Three sisters needs full sun and a sheltered position. Sweetcorn is wind-pollinated and does not set cobs well in a draughty spot. A bed at least 3 by 3 m gives enough plants for the corn to pollinate reliably. Rich, moisture-retentive soil suits all three crops.

In the UK, wait until late May or early June before sowing or planting outdoors. All three crops are frost-tender. Sweetcorn can be started indoors in 9 cm pots in April for transplanting in late May. Climbing beans and squash are best sown directly once soil temperature reaches 15 degrees Celsius, or started indoors two weeks before planting.

Plant sweetcorn plants in a grid 45 cm apart. The block planting improves pollination compared to a single row. Once the corn is 15 to 20 cm tall, sow two or three climbing bean seeds at the base of each sweetcorn plant. The beans will use the corn as a support as they grow.

Sow or plant squash around the edges of the corn block, about 60 cm from the nearest corn plant. As the squash vines spread outward, they cover the bare ground between and beyond the corn planting. Leave paths for access so you can harvest without walking on the bed.

attrs.title: UK-adapted versions
attrs.body: In cooler UK summers, replace sweetcorn with tall climbing bean wigwam frames and pair them with lower-growing beans and squash. This gives a fully productive system without the sweetcorn risk. Alternatively, use a heritage sweetcorn variety bred for cool climates (look for varieties with 60-day maturity periods rated for UK conditions). Traditional companion planting claims for three sisters include reduced pest pressure on beans via squash leaf chemicals. Modern trials show inconsistent results; treat the pest-suppression benefit as a secondary consideration, not the reason to grow it.

content.text: Harvest climbing beans as they reach picking size from July onwards. Pick regularly to keep the plants producing. Sweetcorn is ready when the silks (the thread-like tassels at the end of the cob) turn brown and a kernel pressed releases milky juice. Squash and winter pumpkins are left until October, once the skins have hardened and the stalk has dried.

Cut the bean plants at the soil surface in October. Do not dig out the roots: the nitrogen-fixing root nodules stay in the soil and release nitrogen as they decompose over winter. Chop the corn stalks and squash vines and add them to the compost heap or leave them as a surface mulch over the bed.
